title: Customers Who Never Order
statement:
Two tables record a shop's customers and their orders:

- `Customers(id, name)`: one row per customer; `id` is unique. Two customers may have the same `name`.
- `Orders(id, customerId)`: one row per order; `id` is unique, and `customerId` always names a row of `Customers`. A customer may have many orders.

Report the customers who have no row at all in `Orders`, one row per such customer, in a single column named `Customers` holding the customer's `name`. Rows may come in any order.
constraints: Orders.customerId is never null and always exists in Customers
reference:
WITH buyers AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT customerId
  FROM Orders
)
SELECT c.name AS Customers
FROM Customers AS c
WHERE c.id NOT IN (SELECT b.customerId FROM buyers AS b);
brute:
SELECT c.name AS Customers
FROM Customers AS c
LEFT JOIN Orders AS o
  ON o.customerId = c.id
WHERE o.id IS NULL
notes:
## Intuition

A customer qualifies when their `id` never shows up as a `customerId` in `Orders`. So first collect the set of ids that did order, then keep the customers outside that set. Both steps are plain set operations, which a subquery expresses directly: `id NOT IN (the buyers)`.

## Approach

1. `buyers`: the distinct `customerId` values found in `Orders`, i.e. everyone who ordered at least once.
2. Read `Customers` (alias `c`) and keep a row only when `c.id` is **not in** `buyers`.
3. Output the name under the required column name `Customers`.

## Example 1, step by step

- `Orders` has customerIds 3 and 1, so `buyers` = {3, 1}.
- Joe (id 1) is in `buyers`: dropped.
- Henry (id 2) is not: kept.
- Sam (id 3) is in `buyers`: dropped.
- Max (id 4) is not: kept.

The result is Henry and Max.

## Complexity

- Time: O(C + O) for C customers and O orders when the membership test uses a hash or index; O(C · O) if the database scans `buyers` for each customer.
- Space: O(O) for the set of buyers.

## Pitfalls

- `NOT IN` returns no rows at all if the subquery contains a `null`; here `customerId` is never null, but with nullable columns `NOT EXISTS` is the safe choice.
- Comparing against `Orders.id` instead of `Orders.customerId` mixes up order ids with customer ids.
- An inner join finds the customers who **did** order; the join-based answer needs a `LEFT JOIN` plus `WHERE o.id IS NULL`.
- Selecting `DISTINCT name` would merge two different customers who share a name.

## Clauses

| Name | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `buyers` | each `customerId` that has at least one order |
| `c` | `Customers`, the rows being filtered |
| `b` | `buyers` inside the membership subquery |
| `Customers` (output) | the name of a customer with no orders |

narration.1: The first stage collects the customers who ordered at least once.
narration.2: DISTINCT keeps each ordering customer once, however many orders they placed.
narration.5: Report each surviving customer's name under the column name Customers.
narration.6: Every customer is a candidate, so the query reads the whole Customers table.
narration.7: Keep a customer only when their id is missing from the set of buyers.
